subsection: 8. Immigration patterns and policies in Britain and France; multi-racial Britain

notes.h: Background and key ideas: why migration happened
notes.b: After 1945 both Britain and France needed workers and both ruled or had ruled overseas peoples, so people from the colonies moved to the old imperial centres. Four ideas run through this topic and are used in the same sense throughout.
points: Britain after 1945 had labour shortages in reconstruction, the new National Health Service, transport and industry, and its empire was turning into a Commonwealth (a group of independent states linked to Britain), so many colonial subjects held British status.
France also needed labour for reconstruction and the post-war boom. It had colonies and territories in North and West Africa, and Algeria was treated as part of France until independence in 1962.

The Second World War had discredited racist ideas, because the Nazis had shown where they led. Even so, colour prejudice persisted in both societies, and this is the setting for the conflicts that follow.

Racism means treating people as inferior or different because of their race or colour. It shows itself in prejudice (hostile attitudes), discrimination (unfair treatment in jobs or housing) and violence.
Cultural diversity means many cultures, religions and languages living within one society, which is what migration produced in both countries.
Identity is how migrants and their children saw themselves, often caught between the culture of their family's origin and the host society they lived in.

Assimilation is the expectation that migrants adopt the majority culture, which was the French approach. Multiculturalism, or integration with diversity, accepts that distinct cultures can continue within a common framework, which became the British approach.
notes.tip: Define racism, cultural diversity, identity and assimilation in your own words early in an answer and use them as the exam uses them. Remember that assimilation is the French model and multiculturalism the British one.

notes.b: Britain's post-war labour shortage and the Commonwealth citizenship laws brought large numbers of migrants from the Caribbean and South Asia. They came because there was work in Britain and because the law let them in.
points: The British Nationality Act of 1948 made citizens of the UK and Colonies and of Commonwealth countries British subjects, with the right to enter and settle in Britain.

The SS Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury on 22 June 1948 with about 1,000 passengers, most of them from Jamaica and other Caribbean islands, and it became the symbol of the start of Caribbean migration.

Post-war labour shortages led Britain to recruit workers in the Caribbean in the 1950s, for example for the National Health Service (founded in 1948) and London Transport, and poor prospects at home made the offer attractive.
Migration from India and Pakistan grew in the 1950s and later included Bangladesh, with many migrants from Punjab and Gujarat settling in Birmingham, Leicester, Bradford and London.
Migrants were concentrated in a few big cities and industrial areas, especially London, the West Midlands and Yorkshire, where the jobs were.
Most migrants held Commonwealth citizenship, so they had the right to vote and to live in Britain, but they still faced discrimination in housing and jobs.

Caribbean migrants met a colour bar (a refusal to let rooms to black people) in lodgings. In Notting Hill the landlord Peter Rachman became notorious in the 1950s for overcrowded, exploitative lettings to newcomers.
Migration rose sharply in 1961–62 because migrants rushed to enter Britain before the 1962 Act took effect and restricted entry.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph on Commonwealth migration, give the cause (labour shortage), the 1948 Act, Windrush, recruitment, settlement and discrimination, each as a dated statement.

notes.h: Racism and the first race riots, 1958–1959
notes.b: As migrants settled, hostility from some of the white population turned to violence in 1958. These were the first major riots about race in post-war Britain, and they pushed the question of racism into politics.
points: In August 1958 disturbances broke out in Nottingham, and in late August and September 1958 white youths attacked West Indian residents in Notting Hill, in serious racial violence.
The disturbances were caused by overcrowded housing and competition for jobs and housing, and by far-right agitation in the area, such as Oswald Mosley's Union Movement and the White Defence League.

The Trinidad-born journalist Claudia Jones organised an indoor Caribbean carnival in London in January 1959, a response that celebrated Caribbean culture and became a precursor of the Notting Hill Carnival.
Kelso Cochrane, an Antiguan-born carpenter, was murdered in a racist attack in Notting Hill in May 1959, and his death increased pressure for a legal response to racism.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the 1958 Notting Hill riots (white attacks on West Indians) with the 1981 riots (young people against the police) or the Notting Hill Carnival (1966). For a document on 1958, work out who, where, when, the cause and what followed.

notes.h: Restrictive laws and the rise of anti-immigrant politics, 1962–1979
notes.b: From 1962 governments began to restrict entry, and public debate treated migration as a problem. Extremist groups grew, and so did campaigns against them.
points: The Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962 introduced employment vouchers, which restricted the entry of Commonwealth citizens who had no job arranged in Britain. The Irish were not covered because of the Common Travel Area.
In February 1968 a new Commonwealth Immigrants Act was passed through Parliament in a few days to restrict the entry of Kenyan Asians holding British passports, who faced discrimination in Kenya.

Enoch Powell, a Conservative MP, spoke at a Conservative meeting in Birmingham on 20 April 1968, warning that continued immigration would lead to violence. Edward Heath dismissed him from the Shadow Cabinet the next day, but some London dockers marched in his support.
The speech is known as the 'rivers of blood' speech because it referred to the Tiber 'foaming with much blood', though Powell did not use the phrase itself.
The Immigration Act of 1971 introduced patriality, the right of abode (the right to live in Britain freely) for those with a parent or grandparent born in Britain. It came into force in 1973.

President Idi Amin ordered Asians out of Uganda in August 1972, giving them 90 days to leave. About 27,000 settled in Britain, many holding British passports, helped by the Ugandan Asian Resettlement Board.

The National Front, founded in 1967, campaigned for an end to immigration but never won a parliamentary seat. Its clashes with opponents included the Battle of Lewisham in August 1977 and the death of the teacher Blair Peach at an anti-NF protest in Southall in April 1979.

Rock Against Racism (1976) and the Anti-Nazi League (1977) organised counter-campaigns against the National Front. Overall, migration was framed as a problem and entry was restricted, while the rights of those already settled were protected by law.
notes.tip: Keep the two kinds of law apart: the Commonwealth Immigrants Acts and the 1971 Act control entry, while the Race Relations Acts tackle discrimination. Powell's speech is 1968, after the Kenyan Asians, not 1962, and he was dismissed, not defeated.

notes.h: Anti-discrimination law: the Race Relations Acts, 1965–1976
notes.b: While entry was being restricted, Parliament also made discrimination against people already living in Britain illegal. Each Act widened the ban and set up a body to promote it.
points: The Race Relations Act of 1965 banned discrimination on grounds of colour, race or ethnic or national origins in public places, and it created the Race Relations Board.
The Race Relations Act of 1968 extended the ban to housing, employment and services, which were the areas where migrants had faced the colour bar, and it created the Community Relations Commission.
The Race Relations Act of 1976 extended the law to indirect discrimination (rules that look neutral but disadvantage one group) and created the Commission for Racial Equality.
The laws were enforced through complaints and conciliation, and critics argued that they were limited because discrimination was difficult to prove in practice.
Home Secretary Roy Jenkins said in 1966 that integration should mean equal opportunity accompanied by cultural diversity, not assimilation, and this set the direction of British policy.
notes.tip: Strong answers separate laws that restrict entry from laws that outlaw discrimination, and give the date and the new body for each Race Relations Act. Ordinary Level questions ask what the 1965 Act banned.

notes.b: By the early 1980s many young black people faced unemployment, discrimination in jobs and housing, and tense relations with the police. In 1981 these tensions exploded in riots.
points: Young black people suffered high unemployment in the early 1980s as well as discrimination in jobs and housing, which left many with little stake in society and fed resentment.

Stop and search under the 'sus' laws (the Vagrancy Act of 1824, which let police stop people on suspicion) was used heavily against young black men, and many black residents saw it as harassment. The law was repealed in 1981.
The Brixton riots of 10–12 April 1981 followed Operation Swamp 81, in which police stopped and searched nearly a thousand people in about a week, mostly young black men. Hundreds were injured.
Riots broke out in Toxteth in Liverpool and Moss Side in Manchester in July 1981, as well as in other cities. Police used CS gas on the British mainland for the first time in Toxteth.
The Scarman Report of November 1981 (by Lord Scarman) named racial disadvantage, unemployment and poor relations between police and community as the causes of the riots.
Scarman rejected the idea that the police were institutionally racist (racist in their rules and culture), but accepted that individual officers had acted improperly.

Scarman recommended community policing and consultation, so that police would work with local people. The Police and Criminal Evidence Act of 1984 reformed police powers, and the report was one influence on it among others.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the 'sus' law (stop and search under an 1824 Act) with Operation Swamp 81 (the police operation before Brixton). For achievements against limits, the Scarman Report is among the best evidence, with its findings and its reforms.

notes.b: By the 1980s Britain had large Caribbean, Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi communities, and their culture changed British life in music, food, religion and politics. Their presence also caused tension, as the Rushdie affair showed.
points: Caribbean communities shaped British music, including reggae, ska and calypso, and Caribbean food and festivals became part of urban life.
Notting Hill Carnival began as a street festival in 1966 and grew into one of the largest street festivals in Europe.
Muslims from South Asia built mosques in the 1960s and 1970s, and Sikh and Hindu communities built gurdwaras (Sikh places of worship) and temples in Birmingham, Leicester and London.
Multiculturalism became British policy, supported by local councils and the Race Relations Acts, which encouraged recognition of distinct cultures within a common framework of laws.
The Rampton Report (1981) and the Swann Report (1985) on the education of ethnic minority children argued that schools should recognise those children's needs.
Black and Asian candidates entered Parliament: Diane Abbott, Paul Boateng, Bernie Grant and Keith Vaz were elected in 1987.

The Rushdie affair of 1988–89 showed the tension between religious identity and freedom of expression. Copies of The Satanic Verses (1988) were burned in Bradford in January 1989, and Ayatollah Khomeini issued a fatwa (a religious ruling) against Salman Rushdie in February 1989.
notes.tip: Prepare three areas of impact (music and food, religion, politics) and at least one problem, which is the Rushdie affair, treated as a clash of identity and free speech.

notes.h: France: migration from Europe and Africa, 1945–1974
notes.b: France also recruited workers after 1945, but its migrants came from southern Europe and from its former colonies in North and West Africa. Many of them lived in very poor conditions, and the Algerian war cast a long shadow over them.
points: Post-war reconstruction created labour shortages, and the state set up the National Immigration Office (ONI) in 1945 to recruit. Migrants came from Italy, Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria and West Africa and worked in factories, mines and construction.
Algerians had French status until independence in 1962 and could move freely between Algeria and France, so their movement to the mainland was not immigration in the legal sense before then.

Many migrants lived in bidonvilles, shanty towns on the edges of French cities, such as Nanterre near Paris, in the 1950s and 1960s. Later migrants were housed on housing estates and in state-backed hostels for migrant workers.
On 17 October 1961 Paris police under Maurice Papon attacked an Algerian demonstration against a curfew. Dozens at least were killed, and the number remains disputed.

Algerian migration continued after 1962 and brought the legacy of the Algerian war into French politics. The harkis, Algerians who had served in the French army, came to France as refugees rather than as labour migrants and faced hostility and poor housing.
notes.tip: Link French immigration to the colonial past, especially Algeria, for extra credit. Remember that harkis came as refugees, and bidonvilles (shanty towns) are not the same as banlieues (suburbs).

notes.h: France: the halt to labour migration and its consequences, 1974–1980s
notes.b: The economic downturn of the 1970s ended the recruitment of workers, but it did not end migration, because families then joined those already in France. This produced a new generation that was born and raised in France.
points: In July 1974 the French government suspended labour immigration, which stopped new recruitment of workers but not the arrival of families.
In 1976 the government allowed family reunification for migrants who had been living in France, so wives and children joined them and migrants settled permanently.
After 1977 the government offered payments to migrants who agreed to go home, but few accepted, with little effect.

Migrants from North and West Africa raised a second generation, the 'beurs' (the French-born children of North African migrants), who grew up in the banlieues (the suburbs around big cities) and by the 1980s were a focus of French debate about integration.
notes.tip: The 1974 halt stopped new labour migration, not family arrivals, and family reunification in 1976 is why the migrant population kept growing. Exam questions on France ask why migrants came, where they lived, the 1974 halt, family reunification and the second generation.

notes.h: The French model: assimilation and laïcité
notes.b: France treated migrants very differently from Britain. Its model rested on the idea that the state deals with individual citizens, not with ethnic or religious groups.
points: The French model of integration was based on universal citizenship: all citizens were equal before the law, and the state did not recognise ethnic or religious communities as such.
Assimilation meant that migrants were expected to adopt the French language, values and civic practices, and to keep their ethnic identities in private.
The law separating church and state in 1905 established laïcité, state secularism, which shaped how public religious expression was regulated. Laïcité is secularism, not assimilation itself.
France collected no statistics by ethnic origin, which meant that discrimination was harder to measure and debate than in Britain.
The Pleven law of 1972 was France's main anti-racist legislation, and it made incitement to racial hatred a criminal offence.
notes.tip: Do not mix up assimilation (France) with integration or multiculturalism (Britain). Use the missing ethnic statistics and the Pleven law as points of comparison with the British Race Relations Acts.

notes.b: The two countries faced similar pressures but responded in different ways. A good comparison pairs a similarity or difference in one country with the matching fact from the other.
points: Similarity: both states restricted immigration in the 1970s, Britain with the Acts of 1962, 1968 and 1971 and France with the halt of 1974.

Similarity: both had far-right parties that gained support by the late 1970s and 1980s, both had racial violence in urban areas, and both saw discrimination and the concentration of migrants in poor housing.

Difference: most migrants to Britain were Commonwealth citizens with a legal right of entry, while migrants to France came from southern Europe as well as North and West Africa, and Algerians had a distinct legal status until 1962.
Difference: Britain developed multiculturalism, which recognised ethnic groups, while France used assimilation, which recognised individuals as citizens.

Difference: Britain monitored ethnic groups, which let it measure discrimination, while France collected no ethnic statistics. Britain also passed three Race Relations Acts, while France's main anti-racist law was the Pleven law of 1972.
Difference: Britain's migrants came largely from former colonies in the Caribbean and South Asia, and France's from its former North African and West African colonies.
notes.tip: A Higher Level essay on race relations in Britain and France scores best with a judgement at the start and dated points from both countries. Treating only Britain scores poorly.

notes.h: Assessment: integration and exclusion in Britain and France
notes.b: Both countries tried to integrate migrants, with real achievements and real limits. Historians judge each model by how far it ended disadvantage.
points: Achievement: Britain's anti-discrimination laws gave migrants a legal basis for challenging discrimination in jobs, housing and public services.
Limit: the laws did not end disadvantage, and the 1981 riots showed that unemployment and police practices remained sources of conflict.
Achievement: France's universal citizenship gave second-generation migrants a legal claim to French nationality, and many took part fully in French public life.
Limit: the assimilation model made it difficult to recognise ethnic discrimination, and the banlieues showed the tensions it created.
Contemporary view: many politicians in both countries saw migration mainly as an economic and security problem, while migrant communities often saw discrimination as the main issue.

Later view: scholars contrast Britain's race-relations model, which counted ethnic groups and tackled discrimination through the law, with France's republican model, which counted no one by origin. Each has been criticised for failing to end disadvantage.
notes.tip: Achievements against limits and contemporary against later views are rewarded as paired points, and the Scarman Report and the Race Relations Acts are the best evidence for Britain.

keyTerms.definition: The belief that people can be ranked by race and treated differently on that basis, expressed in discrimination, violence and exclusion.
The presence of many cultures, languages, religions and traditions within one society, which post-war migration brought to Britain and France.
A person's sense of who they are, shaped by ethnicity, nationality, religion, language and place, and often contested by migrants and their children.
The expectation that migrants and minorities adopt the language, values and civic culture of the majority society.
The policy of recognising and supporting distinct cultures and communities within one state, as developed in Britain from the 1960s.
The Immigration Act of 1971 concept that gave the right of abode in Britain to people with a parent or grandparent born there.
A makeshift shanty settlement on the edge of a French city, where many migrant workers lived in poor conditions after the Second World War.
The French principle of state secularism, established by the 1905 law separating church and state, which keeps public institutions free of religious influence.
The right of migrant workers to bring spouses and children to join them, as allowed in France from 1976 after labour migration was halted.
The suburban areas on the edge of French cities, with large housing estates where many migrant families lived.
The British laws of 1962 and 1968 that restricted the right of Commonwealth citizens to enter and settle in Britain.
